newsitem.title: UK: Body Shop profits up but U.S. business still slow.
newsitem.headline: Body Shop profits up but U.S. business still slow.

text.p: The cosmetics retailer Body Shop International Plc Thursday said profits jumped 30 percent in the first half, driven by strong growth in Asia that more than offset steeper losses in the United States.

Pretax profits for the six months through August 31 rose to 11.8 million pounds ($19.2 million) from 9.1 million pounds ($14.8 million) in the comparable 1995 period. Retail sales grew 13 percent to 275.5 million pounds ($448.3 million).
Chairman Gordon Roddick cited "strong growth in Asian markets and regeneration in Australia" but noted the United States had seen a slowdown, producing a bigger loss.
The retailer, which promotes recycling and markets itself as environmentally and socially conscious, has expanded from a single shop in 1976 to nearly 1,436 stores in 46 countries.

Losses in the United States grew to 3.4 million pounds ($5.5 million) from 2.4 million pounds ($3.9 million) in the 1995 period. Sales at stores open at least a year fell 4 percent, compared with an 8 percent drop in the 1995 period.

Last year Body Shop launched a marketing campaign to raise its profile in the United States and it recently hired a new U.S. chief executive, Steen Kanter, who had helped Swedish furniture retailer IKEA bolster its U.S. performance.
Roddick said sales in the competitive U.S. retail market were improving but it was a slow process.
"I think what we have is a long, slow, gradual improvement," he said in a telephone interview. "We're still looking towards a long term success in the USA."
The company is trying to broaden its appeal and has introduced new skin care products aimed at women in their 30s. It is also experimenting with new store formats.

Profits surged 40 percent to 6.5 million pounds ($10.6 million) in Asia, and the region accounted for roughly half of the 63 new shops opened in the first half of the company's fiscal year, including its first outlets in the Philippines.
Sales in Britain were sluggish, growing just 1 percent in the first half.
